paragraphs: The application side of graceful shutdown, from the C++ example; one SIGTERM, the only signal Kubernetes sends before SIGKILL, drives all of it. (1) The SIGTERM handler only stores an atomic flag, which is async-signal-safe: no locks, no allocation, no destructors. Drogon installs its own SIGTERM handler that quits at once, so the example replaces it after initialisation with registerBeginningAdvice. /readyz answers 503 once the flag is set, which removes the pod from the Service endpoints while the process keeps serving the requests already routed to it.

(2) A watcher thread does the rest outside signal context: it sees the flag, keeps serving for DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS (5 s in Example 21; it plays the part of a preStop sleep) so the endpoint removal propagates, waits up to 20 seconds for the RAII InFlightGuard count to reach zero, and calls app().quit(), which stops the listeners so run() returns. (3) main() joins the watcher, closes the libpq pool and returns 0, inside the 30-second grace period. std::stop_token and std::jthread extend the same pattern to worker threads such as Kafka consumers: the watcher calls request_stop() after it sees the flag, never inside the handler. Deterministic destruction makes the teardown order predictable.

paragraphs: Write-back from Example 25: PUT /write-back/metrics/{id} stores the payload in Redis under metric:<id> with a one-hour TTL (a queued write has to outlive a database outage), adds the key to the writeback:dirty set and answers 202 Accepted: the write is queued, not yet durable. A background std::thread wakes every two seconds, reads the dirty set, upserts each metric into Postgres with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and removes the key from the set only after the upsert succeeds, so a failed write stays dirty and is retried on the next cycle.

Retries are bounded: a per-key counter parks a key on writeback:failed after five failed attempts, with its value still in the cache and an error in the log, and the cycle time backs off to four and then eight seconds while flushes fail. The upsert makes a repeated flush harmless. The flusher has its own libpq connection, separate from the request handlers', and main() joins it after the shutdown flag is set (Appendix H). The risk is the one every write-back carries: a write that was acknowledged but not yet flushed is lost if Redis loses it, so keep write-back for data that tolerates that window, such as metrics.

ops.text: Recap of App H in the failure-mode context: pod shutdown is itself a failure mode that graceful drain converts into a non-failure. The C++ disposability discipline of Example 21 (one SIGTERM, an async-signal-safe flag, /readyz answering 503, the drain delay, a bounded in-flight wait, app().quit(), the pool closed and exit 0) is what makes rolling deploys clean.
